name: Ghost Escape from Side Control
description: Learn the Ghost Escape from Side Control in BJJ. Expert guide covering turning mechanics, knee threading, and direct guard recovery techniques for all levels.
overview:
The Ghost Escape from Side Control is a turn-away escape that recovers directly to open guard rather than stopping at turtle. Where the standard ghost escape uses rotational movement to reach hands and knees, this variation threads the near knee through during the turn to establish a leg barrier between you and the opponent, landing in open guard with feet engaged. The technique exploits the same counterintuitive principle of turning in the direction the crossface pushes you, but adds the critical knee insertion that bypasses turtle entirely and denies the top player the back attack opportunities that turtle exposure creates.

The strategic value of this escape lies in its end position. Recovering to open guard rather than turtle eliminates the most dangerous phase of the standard ghost escape, where the bottom player must defend back takes from turtle before recovering guard. By threading the knee during the turn itself, you skip turtle and arrive in a guard position with offensive options immediately available. This makes the technique particularly valuable against opponents who are skilled at following ghost escape rotations to establish back control.

The primary difficulty is the precision required during the knee threading phase. The turning motion must create enough separation for the near knee to slide between your body and the opponent's chest, which demands precise timing and hip mechanics. If the knee insertion fails mid-turn, you end up in the standard ghost escape turtle position rather than guard, which is the most common counter outcome. The technique works best when the opponent's hip pressure is committed to one direction and their weight is concentrated on your upper body rather than your hips, giving your lower body the freedom needed to thread the knee barrier.
conditions: Opponent has established side control with crossface pressure directed away from you
Your far arm is free and not trapped by opponent's control or your own body
Near-side arm can create a frame against opponent's hip or waist to block their follow
Opponent's hip pressure is concentrated on upper body, allowing lower body freedom for knee insertion
Sufficient hip mobility to execute the turn and thread the knee simultaneously

variants_and_adaptations.description: Instead of threading the knee to full open guard, insert the knee as a shield across the opponent's torso during the turn, establishing knee shield half guard. The knee shield provides a more secure initial barrier than open guard and allows you to control distance before transitioning to a full guard system. The reduced range of motion required makes this variant more accessible under heavy pressure.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent follows the turn closely and there is insufficient space for full open guard recovery, or when you prefer a tighter defensive position

variants_and_adaptations.description: During the turning phase, rather than inserting the near knee as a straight barrier, hook both feet inside the opponent's thighs as you face them, landing directly in butterfly guard. This requires faster hip rotation and more precise foot placement but provides immediate sweep threats from butterfly hooks that put the top player on defense the moment you complete the escape.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: Against opponents who drive forward aggressively during the turn, as their forward momentum can be redirected with butterfly hook elevation

variants_and_adaptations.description: In no-gi situations, establish an underhook on the opponent's far arm before initiating the turn. The underhook provides leverage during the rotation and creates additional separation that makes knee threading easier. Upon completing the turn, the underhook converts into wrist control for open guard management.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: In no-gi grappling when the underhook is available and opponent lacks strong crossface control

position_integration: The Ghost Escape from Side Control occupies the advanced tier of the side control escape hierarchy, specifically designed for practitioners who have mastered the standard ghost escape to turtle and want to eliminate the vulnerable turtle phase. It sits alongside the elbow escape, frame-and-shrimp, and bridge-and-roll as a directional alternative that works when traditional toward-opponent escapes are shut down. The technique connects the side control defensive system directly to the open guard offensive system, bypassing the turtle recovery chain entirely. This integration is strategically significant because it converts a purely defensive situation into an immediately offensive one, giving the escaper sweep and submission threats from open guard rather than the defensive survival posture of turtle. The escape complements the standard ghost escape by sharing the same initial setup and timing but diverging at the knee insertion point, allowing practitioners to choose their destination based on how closely the opponent follows the turn.

attacker.name: Ghost Escape from Side Control Attacker
attacker.description: Execute the Ghost Escape from Side Control to open guard. Step-by-step guide covering frame creation, turning mechanics, knee threading, and direct guard recovery.
attacker.overview: Executing the Ghost Escape from Side Control to open guard requires coordinating the standard ghost escape rotation with a precisely timed knee insertion that establishes a guard barrier before you complete the turn. The critical distinction from the standard ghost escape is that your near knee must thread between your body and the opponent during the rotation rather than after it. This simultaneous turn-and-insert mechanic demands more precise hip control and timing than the standard ghost escape but rewards you with immediate guard recovery instead of the vulnerable turtle position. The technique works because the turning motion creates a momentary gap between your midsection and the opponent's chest, and the knee insertion exploits this gap before it closes. Success depends on reading the opponent's weight distribution, timing the turn with a moment of reduced hip pressure, and committing to the knee drive with enough conviction to establish the barrier before the opponent can settle chest-to-chest contact again.
key_principles: Turn into the crossface direction rather than fighting against it, converting opponent's pressure into escape momentum
Thread the near knee during the turn, not after it, to bypass turtle and land directly in guard
Establish a near-side frame before initiating any movement to prevent the opponent from following your turn
Drive hips away explosively during the turn to create the gap needed for knee insertion
Complete the turn and knee insertion as one continuous motion without pausing mid-rotation
Face the opponent immediately upon completing the knee thread to establish guard controls before they can re-pass
setup_requirements: Near-side forearm frame established against opponent's hip or across their waist to create separation
Far arm free and positioned to post on the mat or control opponent's shoulder during the turn
Opponent committed to crossface direction without actively switching sides or transitioning to north-south
Lower body freedom sufficient to rotate hips and thread the knee, meaning opponent's weight is concentrated on your upper body
Mental commitment to execute the full sequence without hesitation once initiated

execution_steps.description: From bottom side control, wedge your near forearm against the opponent's hip bone or across their waist. Keep your elbow tight to your body to prevent arm isolation while creating a structural barrier that blocks the opponent from following your hips when you turn. This frame is the foundation of the entire escape and must be in place before any other movement begins.

execution_steps.action: Position far arm for the turn
execution_steps.description: Place your far hand on the mat beside your far hip as a posting point, or against the opponent's far shoulder to push them away during the turn. This arm serves as the directional guide and balance point for the rotational movement. Avoid extending it where the opponent can isolate it for kimura or americana attacks.

execution_steps.action: Bridge to create initial hip space
execution_steps.description: Execute a short controlled bridge lifting your hips toward the ceiling to momentarily disrupt the opponent's weight distribution. This bridge creates the essential pocket of space between your hips and the mat needed to begin hip rotation. Time the bridge with a moment when the opponent adjusts grips, shifts weight, or initiates a submission setup for maximum effectiveness.

execution_steps.action: Turn hips away with explosive rotation
execution_steps.description: Immediately off the bridge, rotate your hips explosively away from the opponent while your near-side frame pushes their body in the opposite direction. The turn should be sharp and committed with no hesitation. Your hips rotate approximately 90 degrees, bringing your near knee toward the space between your body and the opponent's chest. This is the critical divergence point from the standard ghost escape.

execution_steps.action: Thread near knee through the gap
execution_steps.description: As the turn creates separation between your midsection and the opponent's chest, drive your near knee through this gap and across the opponent's hip line. The knee insertion must happen during the turn while the gap exists, not after you complete the rotation. Push your knee toward their far hip to create maximum barrier width. This is the most technically demanding step and the one that distinguishes this technique from the standard ghost escape to turtle.

execution_steps.action: Square hips to face the opponent
execution_steps.description: Complete the rotation by turning your hips to face the opponent directly. Both legs should now be between you and the opponent with your shins and knees creating a wall that prevents their chest from closing distance. Do not leave your back exposed for any longer than the instant required to complete the turn and knee insertion. Your shoulders should be slightly off the mat with weight on your hips for mobility.

Immediately secure grips on the opponent's sleeves, wrists, or collar while positioning your feet on their hips or creating shin frames across their thighs. Transition directly into active open guard management with distance control and grip fighting rather than remaining in a passive position. Begin threatening sweeps or guard transitions to prevent the opponent from simply re-initiating their pass.

common_counters.counter: Opponent drives hips low and sprawls weight to prevent the initial turn
common_counters.your_response: Abandon the ghost escape and switch to a standard hip escape or elbow escape while their hips are committed low. Their sprawl creates upper body space that traditional escapes can exploit.

common_counters.counter: Opponent follows the turn closely and prevents knee insertion by maintaining chest contact throughout
common_counters.your_response: Accept the turtle position and immediately work guard recovery from turtle via sit-through or granby roll. The turn itself is still valuable even without the knee thread.

common_counters.counter: Opponent transitions to north-south when they feel you beginning to angle your hips away
common_counters.your_response: Abort the ghost escape and switch to north-south escape sequences. The angle change means their pressure is no longer suited for the crossface-based setup this technique requires.

common_counters.counter: Opponent steps over to mount as you expose your hips during the turning phase
common_counters.your_response: Keep the near knee tight to your chest to block the mount transition. If the knee thread is already in progress, accelerate the insertion to establish guard before mount is completed.

common_errors.error: Attempting the turn without establishing the near-side hip frame first
common_errors.consequence: Opponent follows your turn with no barrier, maintaining chest contact and either re-establishing side control or taking your back during the rotation
common_errors.correction: Always establish the near-side forearm frame against the opponent's hip before initiating any turning movement. The frame is what prevents the opponent from following.

common_errors.error: Threading the knee after completing the turn rather than during the turn
common_errors.consequence: The gap between your body and the opponent closes before the knee can be inserted, forcing you into standard turtle rather than guard recovery
common_errors.correction: Initiate the knee drive simultaneously with the hip rotation. The knee must enter the gap while the turn is creating it, not after the turn is complete.

common_errors.error: Pausing mid-rotation with back partially exposed to the opponent
common_errors.consequence: Creates easy back take opportunity while you are in the worst possible intermediate position with no guard barrier and back exposed
common_errors.correction: Commit fully to the entire sequence once initiated. The turn, knee insertion, and facing must be one continuous motion. A half-completed ghost escape is worse than not attempting one.

common_errors.error: Leaving far arm extended during the turn where opponent can isolate it
common_errors.consequence: Opponent catches the extended arm for kimura or americana during the rotation, converting your escape attempt into a submission defense
common_errors.correction: Keep the far arm tight with elbow close to your body during the turn. Use it to post briefly but retract immediately once the rotation begins.

common_errors.error: Failing to immediately establish grips and guard controls after completing the escape
common_errors.consequence: Opponent immediately re-passes your guard because you lack the grips and frames needed to maintain open guard distance control
common_errors.correction: The moment your knee clears and you face the opponent, your hands must be actively securing grips on sleeves, wrists, or collar. Guard without grips is not guard.

common_errors.error: Attempting the escape when opponent's weight is concentrated on your hips rather than upper body
common_errors.consequence: Hip pressure physically prevents the rotation from initiating, and the escape attempt telegraphs your intention without creating any movement
common_errors.correction: Only attempt when you feel the opponent's weight focused on crossface and upper body control. If their hips are heavy on yours, use a standard elbow escape instead.

training_progressions.focus: Isolate the knee insertion movement pattern with a cooperative partner
training_progressions.description: Partner maintains light side control while you practice the hip rotation and knee insertion in slow motion. Focus exclusively on the timing of threading the knee through the gap during the turn, not before or after. Perform 20 repetitions per side per session until the simultaneous turn-and-insert becomes a single coordinated movement.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 2: Full Sequence with Light Resistance
training_progressions.focus: Connect all steps from frame to open guard establishment against compliant pressure
training_progressions.description: Partner maintains side control at 40-50% pressure and allows the escape sequence. Practice the complete chain from frame establishment through bridge, turn, knee thread, and guard recovery. Emphasis on smooth continuous movement with no pauses between steps. Partner provides feedback on timing and gap creation.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 3: Progressive Resistance and Counter Recognition
training_progressions.focus: Execute against increasing resistance and learn to adapt when countered
training_progressions.description: Partner increases resistance to 70-80% and actively attempts to follow the turn or drive hips low. Practice recognizing when the knee thread is available versus when you should accept turtle instead. Develop the decision-making to choose between full guard recovery and turtle fallback based on how closely the opponent follows.

training_progressions.focus: Apply the technique in live side control escape rounds alongside other escape options
training_progressions.description: Full-resistance positional rounds starting from side control bottom. Integrate the ghost escape to guard alongside standard hip escapes, elbow escapes, and bridge-and-roll. Focus on selecting this technique only when conditions are optimal and chaining to alternative escapes when it is countered.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the optimal timing window for initiating the ghost escape to open guard from side control?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The optimal timing is when the opponent shifts weight to their upper body for crossface pressure, adjusts grips, or initiates a submission setup that moves their hip pressure away from your midsection. Any moment when their hips lighten against yours creates the window because the knee thread requires hip freedom to rotate and insert. Attempting against fully settled hip pressure will fail regardless of technique quality.

knowledge_assessment.question: What distinguishes this technique from the standard ghost escape that targets turtle?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The critical distinction is the timing of the knee insertion. In the standard ghost escape, the practitioner completes the full rotation to hands and knees in turtle. In this variant, the near knee threads between the bodies during the turn itself, landing directly in open guard and bypassing turtle entirely. This eliminates back exposure but requires more precise timing and hip mechanics during the rotation phase.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the most critical mechanical detail during the knee threading phase?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The knee must be driven through the gap between your midsection and the opponent's chest while the turn is actively creating that gap, not after the turn is complete. The gap is temporary and closes as the opponent adjusts position, so the knee insertion and hip rotation must occur simultaneously as one integrated movement. Attempting to insert the knee as a separate step after turning results in the gap closing before the knee can clear.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the two most common failure points that cause this escape to result in turtle rather than guard?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The first is threading the knee too late, after the turn has completed and the gap has closed, which forces the standard ghost escape turtle outcome. The second is insufficient frame pressure against the opponent's hip during the turn, which allows them to follow your rotation closely enough that there is no gap for the knee to enter. Both failures convert the technique into the standard ghost escape rather than achieving direct guard recovery.

knowledge_assessment.question: What frame must be established before initiating the turn, and what purpose does it serve?
knowledge_assessment.answer: A near-side forearm frame positioned against the opponent's hip bone or across their waist is essential before turning. This frame serves dual purposes: it creates initial separation between your midsection and the opponent's chest so the turn can begin, and it acts as a barrier that prevents the opponent from following your rotation. Without this frame, the opponent's chest stays connected to your torso throughout the turn, eliminating the gap needed for knee insertion.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent drives heavy crossface pressure as you set up the ghost escape. How does this affect your approach?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Heavy crossface pressure actually assists the ghost escape because you turn in the direction the crossface pushes you rather than fighting against it. The crossface energy converts into turning momentum. However, heavy crossface often comes with reduced hip pressure, which is exactly the condition this technique requires. Use the crossface direction to fuel your turn while exploiting the lighter hip contact to execute the knee thread.

knowledge_assessment.question: The opponent follows your turn closely and blocks the knee insertion. What is your immediate adjustment?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Accept the turtle position rather than forcing a failed knee thread. Complete the standard ghost escape rotation to hands and knees, then immediately work guard recovery from turtle via sit-through, granby roll, or technical stand-up. The turn itself still creates a valuable escape from side control even when the knee insertion fails. Forcing the knee against a closely following opponent wastes energy and may stall you in a vulnerable mid-rotation position.

knowledge_assessment.question: How should you establish open guard controls immediately after completing the knee thread and facing the opponent?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The instant your knee clears and you face the opponent, your primary hand must secure a grip on their nearest sleeve or wrist to prevent them from immediately driving forward to re-pass. Your secondary hand controls their collar, far sleeve, or frames against their shoulder. Your feet should be immediately active on their hips or shins to manage distance. Guard without active grips and foot engagement is not sustainable and will be re-passed within seconds.

attacker.safety_considerations: The ghost escape to open guard is a low-risk technique that does not involve joint manipulation or choking mechanics. The primary safety concern is neck strain during the turning phase if the opponent maintains a strong crossface while you rotate. Avoid forcing the turn against extreme neck pressure; instead, create the frame and bridge first to reduce crossface pressure before initiating rotation. During drilling, both partners should communicate about crossface intensity to prevent cervical strain. The turning motion should be practiced slowly initially to develop proper mechanics before adding speed, as rushing without established frames can result in the opponent landing heavily on your back during the transition. Be cautious with the knee insertion if your partner is driving forward aggressively, as a mistimed knee drive against a heavy opponent can strain the knee joint.

defender.name: Ghost Escape from Side Control Defender
defender.description: Defend the Ghost Escape to guard from side control top. Recognition cues, prevention strategies, and counter-techniques to maintain dominant position.
defender.overview: Defending the Ghost Escape to open guard means preventing the bottom player from threading their knee through during the turning escape and recovering guard directly. As the top player, your primary advantage is that this variant requires more precise mechanics than the standard ghost escape to turtle, meaning there are more points of failure you can exploit. The bottom player needs their near-side frame, a specific weight distribution where your hips are light, and enough space during the turn to drive their knee between the bodies. Your defensive strategy centers on maintaining heavy hip-to-hip contact to deny the rotation space, recognizing the turn initiation within the first fraction of a second, and either preventing the turn entirely or following it so closely that the knee thread is impossible and they default to turtle. The key insight is that denying the knee insertion is as valuable as stopping the turn completely, because forcing them to turtle instead of guard puts them in a position where you can attack their back.
key_principles: Maintain heavy hip-to-hip contact to deny the rotational space needed for the knee thread
Recognize the turn initiation immediately by feeling for hip rotation away from you rather than toward you
Follow the turn with your chest to close the gap the bottom player needs for knee insertion
Strip near-side frames proactively since the frame is the prerequisite for the entire escape
Drive weight into the hip frame to collapse it rather than allowing it to create separation
If the turn begins, prioritize closing the gap over trying to flatten them back to side control
recognition_cues: Bottom player establishes a strong forearm frame against your hip rather than framing toward your shoulder or neck
Bottom player's far hand moves to the mat on their far side as a posting point, indicating preparation for rotational movement
Bottom player bridges and immediately angles their hips away from you rather than bridging straight up or toward you
You feel the bottom player stop fighting the crossface direction and instead begin moving with it, suggesting they plan to use your pressure as turning momentum

defensive_options.action: Drive hips low and heavy against opponent's hips to prevent the initial rotation from starting
defensive_options.when_to_use: Preemptively when you feel the opponent establishing the near-side hip frame that signals ghost escape setup
defensive_options.if_successful: Opponent remains pinned with insufficient hip space to initiate the turn, neutralizing the escape before it begins
defensive_options.risk: Over-committing hip weight forward may reduce your crossface pressure, opening space for traditional hip escapes toward you

defensive_options.action: Follow the turn by driving your chest onto opponent's back and closing the gap to prevent knee insertion
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the opponent has committed to the turn and their hips are already rotating away from you
defensive_options.if_successful: Opponent reaches turtle instead of guard, giving you back attack opportunities from turtle top position
defensive_options.risk: If you follow too aggressively without controlling their hips, they may complete the knee thread before you can close the gap

defensive_options.action: Transition to north-south by circling toward opponent's head when you feel them angling hips away
defensive_options.when_to_use: Early in the escape attempt when the opponent's hips just begin to angle but before the explosive turn
defensive_options.if_successful: Cut off the escape angle entirely by changing the control position, resetting all escape attempts from a new angle
defensive_options.risk: The north-south transition creates momentary hip separation that a quick opponent may exploit to accelerate their turn

defensive_options.action: Collapse the near-side hip frame by driving your weight through it and swimming your arm inside to underhook
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you recognize the frame establishment that precedes the escape, before any turning movement begins
defensive_options.if_successful: Eliminate the frame that makes the escape possible, forcing the opponent to re-establish before they can attempt the escape again
defensive_options.risk: Swimming for the underhook momentarily reduces chest pressure, which may create space for alternative escape paths

favorable_outcomes.how: Prevent the turn entirely by maintaining heavy hip-to-hip contact and proactively collapsing the near-side frame when you feel it being established. Drive your hips low and forward the instant you recognize rotational hip movement, flattening the bottom player before the turn develops any momentum.

When the turn is already committed, follow it aggressively by driving your chest onto the opponent's back and closing the gap between bodies so the knee cannot thread through. Accept the transition to turtle top where you have back attack opportunities, which is significantly better than allowing direct guard recovery.

common_errors.error: Maintaining only crossface pressure without hip-to-hip contact in side control
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player has the hip freedom needed to initiate the rotation and thread the knee, making the ghost escape to guard available as a high-percentage option
common_errors.correction: Keep hips low and in direct heavy contact with opponent's hips at all times. Your hip weight is what prevents both the rotation and the knee insertion.

common_errors.error: Attempting to flatten the opponent after the turn is already committed rather than following to turtle
common_errors.consequence: You lose side control without establishing any alternative dominant position, and the opponent completes guard recovery while you fight a lost battle
common_errors.correction: If the turn has momentum, follow it to turtle top rather than trying to reverse it. Turtle top gives you back attacks; letting them recover guard gives you nothing.

common_errors.error: Allowing the near-side hip frame to stay established without addressing it
common_errors.consequence: The frame creates the separation needed for the turn and acts as a barrier preventing you from following, both of which enable the escape
common_errors.correction: Actively strip or collapse the hip frame by driving your weight through it or swimming your arm inside for an underhook. Do not allow frames to persist.

common_errors.error: Reacting slowly to the turn initiation and missing the early counter window
common_errors.consequence: By the time you respond, the gap has been created and the knee is already threading through, making it too late to prevent guard recovery
common_errors.correction: Train immediate reflexive responses to rotational hip movement. The counter window is less than one second from when rotation begins. Recognition speed is the single most important defensive attribute.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the earliest cue that the opponent is setting up the ghost escape to guard rather than a standard hip escape?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The earliest cue is the opponent establishing a forearm frame against your hip rather than against your shoulder or neck. Traditional hip escapes use shoulder frames to create space to shrimp toward you, while the ghost escape to guard uses the hip frame to prevent you from following the turn away from you. The frame placement tells you which direction the escape will go.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why is hip-to-hip pressure more important than crossface for preventing this specific escape?
knowledge_assessment.answer: This escape actually uses the crossface pressure to generate turning momentum by rotating in the direction the crossface pushes. More crossface pressure can inadvertently fuel the escape. Hip-to-hip pressure, however, directly prevents the hip rotation that initiates the turn and eliminates the space needed for knee insertion. Without hip freedom, the escape cannot begin regardless of how strong the bottom player's frames are.

knowledge_assessment.question: The opponent has already begun turning and you cannot stop the rotation. What is your best response?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Follow the turn aggressively by driving your chest onto their back and closing the gap between your bodies so their knee cannot thread through. Your goal shifts from preventing the escape to preventing the guard recovery. If you close the gap successfully, they arrive in turtle rather than guard, giving you back attack opportunities from turtle top, which is a much better outcome than allowing direct guard recovery.

knowledge_assessment.question: How should you adjust your side control maintenance against an opponent known to use this escape?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Prioritize maximum hip-to-hip contact with your weight distributed more toward their hips than their upper body. Proactively strip any near-side hip frames the moment they appear. Reduce reliance on heavy crossface pressure since it can fuel the turn. Stay alert for the bridge-to-rotation combination and be prepared to either drive hips low or immediately follow the turn within the first half-second of rotation.

knowledge_assessment.question: What makes defending this variant different from defending the standard ghost escape to turtle?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The standard ghost escape simply requires stopping the rotation to prevent turtle. This variant adds the knee threading phase, meaning you have a secondary line of defense: even if you cannot stop the turn, you can still prevent the guard recovery by following closely enough to deny the knee insertion. This means following the turn to turtle top is a viable and favorable defensive outcome, whereas against the standard ghost escape, following to turtle is the expected result.

training_progressions.focus: Learn to distinguish ghost escape to guard setups from standard escapes
training_progressions.description: Partner alternates between standard hip escapes, standard ghost escapes to turtle, and ghost escapes to guard at slow speed. Focus on identifying the hip frame placement and rotation direction that signals each escape type. Call out the escape type verbally before the partner completes it.

training_progressions.focus: Practice maintaining hip pressure and collapsing frames to deny escape conditions
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts the ghost escape to guard at moderate speed while you focus on maintaining hip-to-hip contact and immediately addressing any hip frames. Measure success by whether the partner can initiate the turn at all. Reset after each attempt.

training_progressions.focus: Practice following the turn to close the gap and prevent knee insertion
training_progressions.description: Partner executes the ghost escape turn at full speed. You allow the turn but practice following with your chest to deny the knee thread, forcing them to turtle. Focus on gap closing speed and chest-to-back connection during the follow.

training_progressions.focus: Defend all escape types including ghost escape to guard in live rounds
training_progressions.description: Full-resistance side control maintenance rounds where partner uses their complete escape arsenal. Focus on recognizing which escape is being attempted within the first half-second and selecting the appropriate defensive response. Track success rates for each escape type defended.
